title: The Lunch at Chickenland That Turned Into Nando's
dek: In 1987 two colleagues from an electronics firm bought a run-down Portuguese café in Rosettenville, knowing almost nothing about restaurants.

story.event: Buying the Chickenland café in Rosettenville and renaming it Nando's
story.summary: In 1987 Fernando Duarte took his friend and colleague Robbie Brozin to lunch at Chickenland, a run-down Portuguese café in Rosettenville, Johannesburg, known for flame-grilled peri-peri chicken. The two left their jobs at Brozin's father's electronics business, bought the building and the business, and renamed it Nando's; an early, hasty move abroad disappointed them, and Brozin later said they had to learn to adapt to each market.
paragraphs: In 1987 Robbie Brozin was 27, a commerce graduate who by his own account had failed accounting three or four times. He was marketing manager at his father's electronics business, which sold Sanyo hi-fi and video equipment. Its technical manager was Fernando Duarte, who came from Porto and whose family had spent five years in Mozambique and settled in South Africa. The two had known each other since they were about 20 and now worked together. Both, Brozin later said, had grown restless.

Duarte took him to lunch at Chickenland, a Portuguese café in Rosettenville, south of Johannesburg, where chicken was marinated in peri-peri sauce for a day before going on the flame grill. Brozin later called the place "a real broken-down little café" but said, "I knew it in my heart when I tasted the chicken." He put the idea to Duarte: "Why don't we buy this restaurant, fix it up and take it global?"

He has never pretended they knew what they were doing. "We really were naïve to the point of stupidity," he said in 2009. They left their jobs in April 1987, with his father's support, and bought the building and the business. Brozin had imagined himself as an investor who would drop in on Monday mornings to collect the money; instead he was drawn in, and found the restaurant trade hard and full of detail. They wanted to call it Fernando's, could not register the name, and chose Nando's, which was also the name of Duarte's son.

The next lesson came quickly. Within two years they had taken Nando's abroad, and it fell short of what they expected. The biggest mistake, Brozin said, was "thinking you can just take a South African business model and transport it overseas"; each market had different costs and customers. They learnt to adapt, and by 2009 Nando's had some 700 outlets in 26 countries. A Johannesburg Heritage Foundation plaque now marks the corner in Rosettenville where it began.

quote.text: If thou wouldest seek out the nature of a friend, ask it not of any companion of his; but pass a time with him alone, that thou injure not his affairs. Debate with him after a season; test his heart in an occasion of speech.
quote.work: The Instruction of Ptahhotep (and of Ke'gemni)
quote.source_title: The Instruction of Ptah-Hotep and the Instruction of Ke'Gemni, tr. Battiscombe G. Gunn, Project Gutenberg eBook #30508
quote.connection: Ptahhotep advises learning a friend's nature slowly, in time spent alone together and in real conversation. Brozin and Duarte had been friends since their twenties and colleagues before that lunch, so when they bet on a café neither knew how to run, what they did know was each other.

reflection: Brozin is unusually frank that he and Duarte knew almost nothing about restaurants. What they had instead was years of friendship and work side by side, so when the trade turned out to be hard and detailed, each was learning it beside someone whose habits he already knew.

You may not choose a business partner this year, but you are always choosing whom to lean on: a colleague, a friend, a sister or brother. It is worth noticing whom you have actually come to know in ordinary conversation, over time, and giving those people a little more of your trust and your time.
invitation: Have an unhurried conversation today with one colleague or friend you would want beside you in something difficult. Ask how their week is really going, and listen to the end.

research_notes: Price: The Edge (2009) gives about US$100,000, while Wikipedia, citing David Fick's Entrepreneurship in Africa (2002), gives about 80,000 rand; the two are far apart at 1987 exchange rates, so the story does not state a price. Stake: Wikipedia's Brozin article, citing a Harvard Business School interview that returns 403 here, says they first bought 67% and the rest in 1990; the story says only that they bought the building and the business, as the Johannesburg Heritage Foundation plaque puts it. The name: Brozin (2009) says they could not register Fernando's and chose Nando's, also his son's name; the plaque says it was named after Duarte's first-born son; Khaleej Times says after Fernando, known as Nando; the story gives Brozin's account. Ambition: in 2009 Brozin recalled proposing to 'take it global', whereas a 2004 Nando's press release quotes him saying there were 'no real plans for immediate expansion' in the early days; the story keeps his quoted proposal and the documented move abroad within two years, which he described as disappointing. 'Hard and full of detail' paraphrases his 2018 remark to CFO South Africa that the business was 'hard and detailed'. Who discovered the café: the plaque and Khaleej Times say Duarte took Brozin; the 2004 release says Duarte invited him; all agree. Outlet figures (700 in 26 countries) are as reported in 2009 and are not updated. The Zawya release does not name its issuer but quotes Brozin as co-founder of Nando's Chickenland. Ptahhotep's maxim on testing a friend is applied by analogy to a long working friendship.
